data.content_ref: inline:SRC_003 relies on a low 'entropy of the dependency graph' as the decisive test for when decentralization fails to improve resilience, but 'entropy' as stated is only a one-sided criterion: low entropy is claimed to negate decentralization's benefit, yet nothing is said about whether the monolith being compared against also has a low-entropy dependency graph or what entropy threshold makes decentralization *actually better*. Since the monolith with strictly more internal redundancy almost certainly has the *lowest possible* entropy of dependency graph (one big system, internally redundant), using low entropy to argue the decentralized network is 'false' (not more resilient) implies that the monolith fails the same test at least as badly. A covering principle that would distinguish the architectures must explain why *the same* low-entropy property that destroys decentralization's resilience advantage does not equally (or more so) disqualify the monolith the problem asks us to compare against.
